Blog · October 2026

Why walk and talk therapy works

People who have sat in a therapy room and found it hard to speak often assume the problem is them. Sometimes the problem is the room. Two chairs facing each other, sustained eye contact, and an expectation that you will produce words about something painful is a demanding setup, and for some nervous systems it is the wrong one.

What changes on a trail

  1. You are side by side, not face to face. Direct sustained eye contact is a lot of social load, and for people whose early relationships were unsafe it can read as scrutiny rather than attention. Walking removes it without removing the relationship. Plenty of people say the hardest sentence of their life while looking at a trail.
  2. Your body has somewhere to put the activation. Talking about something difficult mobilises energy. In a chair there is nowhere for it to go, so it shows up as a racing heart, a tight chest or the urge to leave. Walking gives that energy an outlet while the conversation continues, which is often the difference between staying with something and shutting down.
  3. Silence stops being awkward. A pause in a room is conspicuous and most people fill it. A pause while walking is just walking. Some of the useful parts of a session happen in those minutes, and the trail makes them easy to leave alone.
  4. The pace is honest. People slow down when they get near something that matters, and speed up when they want past it. That is visible outdoors in a way it is not in a chair, and it is worth noticing out loud.

Who it is not for

Outdoor sessions are not more therapeutic by default, and saying so would be selling something. A trail is a public place. Complete confidentiality is not available on one, and anyone who tells you otherwise is not being careful with you.

If what you need to talk about is something you would not want a passing stranger to catch three words of, that conversation belongs indoors or online. That is not a lesser option; it is the right room for that material.

It is also the wrong format if walking is painful, if the heat is a medical problem for you, or if being outdoors is itself activating. None of that needs explaining or justifying in the consult.

Plenty of people do some of both, and move between them depending on what the week holds.

Questions about walking sessions

Does walk and talk therapy work as well as sitting in an office?

For some people, better, and for some people not at all. It is a format rather than a method: the same approaches apply either way. What changes is how easy it is to stay in the conversation, and that varies by person and by what is being talked about.

Who is walk and talk therapy not a good fit for?

Anyone whose material is too sensitive to risk being overheard in a public place, anyone for whom walking or heat is a problem, and anyone who finds being outdoors activating rather than settling. It is also not the right starting point when someone is in acute crisis.

Do we talk the whole time?

No, and that is part of why it works. Stretches of walking without speaking are normal and are not a sign the session is going badly. The quiet often does more than the talking does.

Is walking outside just a nicer version of a normal session?

It is a different set of trade-offs rather than an upgrade. You gain side-by-side positioning, movement and easier silence. You give up privacy, climate control and the ability to do anything that needs you still and undistracted. Which matters more depends on the work.
